claims.text: Enhanced sampling methods such as metadynamics or umbrella sampling combined with thermodynamic integration can accurately compute melting properties and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced sampling methods can compute these properties more efficiently than traditional DSC measurements or standard molecular dynamics.
High-entropy alloys near melting have complex, disordered multi-principal-element configurations.
The solid–liquid transition in high-entropy alloys involves high free-energy barriers.
Metadynamics or umbrella sampling combined with thermodynamic integration can traverse the solid–liquid transition.
Free-energy-landscape features, including changes in local atomic order and diffusion across the phase boundary, govern the solid–liquid transition.
Changes in local atomic order and diffusion across the phase boundary determine melting thermodynamic properties.
Enhanced sampling adequately samples rare events in the complex energy landscapes of high-entropy alloys.
Adequate rare-event sampling improves convergence of free-energy differences between solid and liquid phases.
Converged solid–liquid free-energy differences allow accurate estimation of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
Enhanced sampling may reduce relative errors by roughly 10–20% compared with conventional techniques.
Traditional calorimetry and conventional molecular dynamics have limitations in capturing the compositional and thermodynamic complexity of high-entropy alloys.
The approach is applicable across a range of high-entropy-alloy compositions near their melting temperatures under equilibrium conditions.
Performance may vary with alloy composition, configurational complexity, and simulation system size.
